Posthomerica.title: Posthomerica
Posthomerica.lead: The Posthomerica is an epic poem in Greek hexameter verse by Quintus of Smyrna. Probably written in the 3rd century AD, it tells the story of the Trojan War, between the death of Hector and the fall of Ilium (Troy). The poem is an abridgement of the events described in the epic poems Aethiopis and Iliou Persis by Arctinus of Miletus, and the Little Iliad by Lesches, all now-lost poems of the Epic Cycle. The first four books, covering the same ground as the Aethiopis, describe the doughty deeds and deaths of Penthesileia the Amazon, of Memnon, son of Eos, and of Achilles; and the funeral games in honour of Achilles.

summaries.heading: Book 1
summaries.text: Quintus dispenses with the customary invocation of the Muses in order to make his first line continue from the end of the Iliad. Book 1 tells of the arrival of the proud Amazon queen Penthesileia, the daughter of Ares, who comes from the Thermodon River with a group of Amazon warriors after accidentally killing her sister while aiming at a stag. She has come to share the hardships of war and to escape her people. The welcome she receives from the hard-pressed Trojans includes Priam's hope that she will save Troy and kill Achilles, although Andromache doubts that she is capable of doing so. Priam prays to Zeus that Penthesileia may return safely, but an eagle carrying a dove appears as an omen foretelling her death. Penthesileia enjoys initial successes in battle, killing Podarces, but is defeated by Achilles, who kills her by impaling her and her horse.

summaries.heading: Book 2
summaries.text: The Trojans debate their situation. Thymoetes is despondent, Priam encouraging. The wise Polydamas' suggestion that Helen should be given back meets with an angry response from Paris. The rest of the book is similar in plan to Book 1. Trojan hopes are raised by the arrival of Priam's nephew Memnon, son of Dawn, and his Ethiopian troops. Like Penthesileia, he is royally entertained, enjoys initial success in the battle, and is defeated by Achilles. Memnon kills Nestor's son Antilochus before Achilles kills him. His divine mother, the Dawn, has his body carried away by the winds and metamorphoses his troops into birds. In her grief Dawn refuses to let the sun rise and retreats to Hades until Zeus persuades her to return. The book closes with mourning, both divine and human.

summaries.heading: Book 3
summaries.text: Apollo warns Achilles to stop the slaughter and, when he defiantly continues, shoots him in the ankle with an arrow. The wound will eventually prove fatal. The Trojans are initially afraid to confront the injured Achilles, but after his death there is a desperate struggle over his body, in which Ajax, son of Telamon, takes the lead on the Greek side. Ajax kills Glaucos, who falls on top of Achilles, and also injures Aeneas, while Odysseus helps him defend the body. Ajax stuns Paris with a rock, forcing him to abandon his attempt to take Achilles' corpse. The Trojans fall back and the body is recovered. Book 3, like Books 1 and 2, ends with mourning. Achilles is lamented by Phoenix, Briseis, the Nereids, and his mother (Thetis), and the preparations for his funeral are described.

summaries.heading: Book 4
summaries.text: The gods react variously to Achilles' death, and the Greeks prepare to resume hostilities. But Thetis wishes to hold funeral games in honor of her son, and in the remainder of the book these competitions are described. They involve all-in wrestling, the long jump, and horse riding, all of which featured in the games of the Roman imperial period; and Nestor's verse encomium of Achilles probably reflects the artistic contests commonly included in games in Quintus' time.

summaries.heading: Book 5
summaries.text: Achilles' armor is displayed by Thetis, and there is a long description of the shield. She offers the armor as a reward for the man who recovered Achilles' body. Ajax (son of Telamon) and Odysseus claim the prize, and the invidious decision between them is left to Trojan prisoners of war. After hearing the speeches, they award the armor to Odysseus. Quintus has narrated the fighting in Book 4 so as to show that this is the wrong decision. Ajax, raging with disappointment, plans to slaughter the Greeks during the night, but Athena diverts his fury against a flock of sheep. Once his madness leaves him, he feels humiliated and kills himself. He is lamented by his half-brother Teucer and his concubine Tecmessa. Odysseus tries to conciliate the army with a patently insincere speech. The book closes with Ajax' funeral, which recalls that of Achilles at the end of Book 3.

summaries.heading: Book 6
summaries.text: Menelaus tests the Greeks' resolve by proposing retreat, but Diomedes threatens to kill anyone who tries to leave before Troy is taken. In response to advice from the seer Calchas that this will not happen unless Achilles' son Neoptolemus is present, Odysseus and Diomedes set sail for Scyros to fetch him. Eurypylus, leader of the Cetaeans, comes with his army to the aid of the Trojans. He is the grandson of Heracles and the son of Telephus, who once fought Achilles. Like Penthesileia in Book 1 and Memnon in Book 2, he is royally received. There is a long description of his shield, which depicts the Labours of Heracles; this complements the description of Achilles' shield in Book 5. The second half of the book tells of various encounters in battle between the Greeks and the Trojans, with Eurypylus leading the Trojan attack and killing many Argive soldiers.

summaries.heading: Book 7
summaries.text: Some of the Greeks hold funerals for Nireus and Machaon, victims of Eurypylus. Machaon's grief-stricken brother Podalirius is offered consolation by Nestor. The Greek forces are driven back to their wall by Eurypylus. A truce allows burial of the dead. Meanwhile Odysseus and Diomedes find Neoptolemus eager to join the war, in spite of the pleading of his mother, Deidamia. They return to Troy just in time to rescue the Greek cause. Neoptolemus is given his father's armor, and he rushes into battle. The book closes with his formal welcome from Phoenix and the Greek commanders. Both sides are now confident of success.

summaries.heading: Book 8
summaries.text: Eurypylus and Neoptolemus lead out their forces, and each is successful in the battle. Eventually they meet, exchange proud words, and fight. Eurypylus is slain. Neoptolemus runs riot, killing so many Trojans that Quintus expresses surprise at his body count. Ares rallies the Trojans but is warned by Zeus not to fight Neoptolemus. Apollo encourages the Trojans, and fierce fighting ensues. Just as the Greeks seem about to break into the city, Ganymede begs Zeus not to let him see Troy's destruction. Zeus hides the city in cloud, and Nestor warns the Greeks not to incur divine anger. They stop fighting, bury their dead, and honor the exploits of Neoptolemus. Both sides keep watch through the night.

summaries.heading: Book 9
summaries.text: The Trojans bury Eurypylus, and Neoptolemus prays at the tomb of his father, Achilles. Deïphobus encourages the fearful Trojans to fight, and both he and Neoptolemus slay countless victims. Finally they meet, but Deïphobus is removed from the battlefield by Apollo. Poseidon supports the Greeks and warns Apollo not to kill Neoptolemus. Calchas reveals that Troy may not be captured without the help of Philoctetes. Odysseus and Diomedes go to fetch him from the island of Lemnos. They find him living in a cave and still suffering from the putrid wound whose stench had caused the Greeks to abandon him. Although Philoctetes considers Odysseus responsible for leaving him behind, he forgives him and is persuaded to accompany them to Troy, where he is cured by Podalirius, honored, and offered compensation.

summaries.heading: Book 10
summaries.text: In an opening similar to that of Book 2, the wise Polydamas advises the Trojans to fight defensively from their walls, but Aeneas is for continuing the battle. Intense fighting ensues. Philoctetes, whose baldric is described at length, shoots many victims with the bow of Heracles and eventually wounds Paris with a poisoned arrow. Paris, mortally wounded, seeks help from Oenone, the wife whom he deserted in favor of Helen. She rejects his plea with scorn. Hera and the Seasons discuss what will happen after his death. Hecuba and Helen lament him, and the remorseful Oenone leaps on his funeral pyre. Paris and Oenone are buried next to one another, with their headstones facing in opposite directions.

summaries.heading: Book 11
summaries.text: The first part of the book tells of the battle on the plain. Aeneas and Eurymachus are urged on by Apollo. The Trojans are driven back by Neoptolemus and his Myrmidons, but Aeneas rallies them. A dust storm settles over the battle. When Athena intervenes on the Greek side, Aphrodite removes Aeneas from the battlefield, and the Trojans retreat within their walls. The second part of the book describes the Greeks' assault on the city on the following day. The Greeks approach the gates under their shields, led by Odysseus, while Ares gives Aeneas the strength to retaliate by throwing huge rocks. Philoctetes shoots at Aeneas, but his shield protects him and the arrow strikes Mimas instead. The result is an impasse.

summaries.heading: Book 12
summaries.text: Prompted by an omen of a hawk and dove, the seer Calchas advises the Greeks to resort to trickery. Odysseus suggests a wooden horse. Neoptolemus and Philoctetes wish to continue fighting, but an omen from Zeus guarantees the plan. Epeius is inspired by Athena to construct the horse. A fight between the gods on opposing sides in the war is quelled by Zeus. Sinon volunteers to stand by the horse and persuade the Trojans to take it inside their city. The rest of the Greeks, with Nestor and Agamemnon, sail away to Tenedos, leaving Sinon as a heavily disfigured messenger. Quintus invokes the Muses to help him list those who entered the horse; among them are Neoptolemus, Menelaüs, Odysseus, Sthenelus, Diomedes, and Philoctetes. When questioned by the Trojans, Sinon maintains his story that the horse is a tribute to Athena Tritogeneia.

summaries.heading: Book 13
summaries.text: As the Trojans sleep, Sinon summons the Greeks. The slaughter begins. Ilioneus vainly begs Diomedes for his life, but Priam is eager to be killed when confronted by Neoptolemus. Hector's young son Astyanax is murdered; his mother, Andromache, begs for death but is taken into slavery. Antenor is spared as reward for past hospitality. Calchas warns the Greeks not to harm Aeneas, who is destined to found a new city. Menelaüs kills Helen's new husband, Deïphobus, but Aphrodite prevents him from killing Helen. Locrian Ajax rapes Cassandra in the temple of Athena, incurring the goddess' wrath. The city is set ablaze. Aethra, Theseus' mother, unexpectedly meets her grandsons. Priam's daughter Laodice prays to be swallowed up by the earth.

summaries.heading: Book 14
summaries.text: The women of Troy are assigned to their new masters. Helen's beauty prevents the Greeks from blaming her. There are general celebrations, with bards singing of the war. Menelaüs forgives Helen. Achilles appears to Neoptolemus in a dream, gives him moral advice, and demands the sacrifice of Polyxena to appease his continuing anger over Briseïs. Her sacrifice, and the misery of her mother Hecuba, are described at length. Hecuba is metamorphosed into a dog made of stone. The voyage gets under way, with very different emotions experienced by the Greeks and the captive women. Athena complains to Zeus of Locrian Ajax' sacrilege and is lent the weapons of storm. The ships are scattered. Ajax is defiant to the end. Many perish on the Capherean Rocks. Poseidon destroys all trace of the Greeks' walls at Troy. The survivors come to land. The Odyssey can begin.

Q102884.label: Mnemosyne
Q102884.description: personification of memory in Greek mythology, mother of the nine muses
Q102884.lead: In Greek mythology, Mnemosyne was one of the Titans, who are the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She was the goddess of memory and the mother of the nine Muses by Zeus.

Q103107.label: Leto
Q103107.description: Greek mythological figure and mother of Apollo and Artemis
Q103107.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Leto is the mother of Apollo and Artemis. She is the daughter of the Titans Coeus and Phoebe, and the sister of Asteria.

Q10350754.label: Poeas
Q10350754.description: Argonaut and friend of Heracles in Greek mythology
Q10350754.lead: In Greek mythology, Poeas, or Poias was a king of Meliboea or Malis (Maleae) and one of the Argonauts.

Q103975.label: Calliope
Q103975.lead: In Greek mythology, Calliope is the Muse who presides over eloquence and epic poetry, so called from the ecstatic harmony of her voice. Hesiod and Ovid called her the "Chief of all Muses".

Q1045730.label: Thersites
Q1045730.description: son of Agrius, Achean warrior in the Trojan War
Q1045730.lead: In Greek mythology, Thersites was a soldier of the Greek army during the Trojan War.

Q1061747.label: Phoenix
Q1061747.description: Greek mythological character, son of Amyntor and tutor of Achilles
Q1061747.lead: In Greek mythology, Phoenix was the son of king Amyntor.

Q106879769.label: Polemusa
Q106879769.lead: In Greek mythology, Polemusa was one of the Amazons, a race of warrior-women. She came with their queen, Penthesilia to the Trojan War.

Q106879772.label: Harmothoe
Q106879772.lead: Harmothoe is the name of two personages in Greek mythology. Harmothoe, the "dark-eyed" Amazonian warrior.

Q106879801.label: Evandre
Q106879801.lead: In Greek mythology, Evandre was one of the Amazons, a race of warrior-women. She came with their queen, Penthesilia to the Trojan War.

Q106879803.label: Thermodosa
Q106879803.lead: In Greek mythology, Thermodosa was one of the Amazons, a race of warrior-women. She came with their queen, Penthesilia to the Trojan War.

Q106879820.label: Clonie
Q106879820.description: Amazon at Troy in Greek mythology
Q106879820.lead: In Greek mythology, Clonie was the 'fair as a goddess' Amazon. She came with their queen, Penthesilia to the Trojan War.

Q106879821.label: Derimacheia
Q106879821.lead: In Greek mythology, Derimacheia was one of the Amazons, a race of warrior-women. She came with their queen, Penthesilia to the Trojan War.

Q1069769.label: Eetion
Q1069769.description: king of Thebe and father of Andromache
Q1069769.lead: In Greek mythology, Eëtion or Eetion is the king of the Anatolian city of Cilician Thebe. He is said to be the father of Andromache, the wife of the Trojan prince Hector.

Q10796858.label: Tecmessa
Q10796858.description: daughter of Teuthras in Greek mythology
Q10796858.lead: In Greek mythology, Tecmessa is a princess from Phrygia, a region in western Asia Minor, daughter of king Teleutas. During the Trojan War Tecmessa's homeland was raided by the Greeks, and Tecmessa herself became a war-prize of Ajax the Greater, one of the strongest Greek warriors.

Q1081453.label: Glaucus
Q1081453.lead: In Greek mythology, Glaucus was a captain in the Lycian army under the command of his close friend and cousin Sarpedon. The Lycians in the Trojan War were allies of Troy.

Q108419.label: Rhea
Q108419.description: female Titan in Greek mythology, mother of Zeus and mother of Hera
Q108419.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhea, Rhia or Rheia was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She was the sister and wife of Cronus, and by him was the mother of Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Zeus.

Q111288806.label: Mygdon
Q111288806.description: eponym of Mygdonia in Greek mythology

Q1134694.label: Scamander
Q1134694.lead: Scamander, also Skamandros or Xanthos (Ξάνθος), was a river god in Greek mythology.

Q1154473.label: Theano
Q1154473.description: priestess of Athena in Troy in Greek mythology
Q1154473.lead: In Greek mythology, Theano was the wife of Antenor and a priestess of Athena at Troy during the Trojan War.

Q1178583.label: Laodice
Q1178583.lead: In Greek mythology, Laodice was the daughter of Priam of Troy and Hecuba. She was described as the most beautiful of Priam's daughters.

Q11921121.label: Aethra
Q11921121.lead: In Greek mythology, Aethra or Aithra was a Troezenian princess and the daughter of King Pittheus.

Q1205276.label: Polydamas
Q1205276.description: Trojan hero, son of Panthoos in the Iliad
Q1205276.lead: In Greek mythology, Polydamas was a lieutenant and friend of Hector during the Trojan War.

Q1206572.label: Podarces
Q1206572.lead: In Greek mythology, Podarces was a son of Iphiclus (son of Phylacus, founder of Phylace) by Diomedeia and the brother of Protesilaus. In some accounts, he and his brother were called the sons of Phylacus and Astyoche instead.

Q120831.label: Eurypylus
Q120831.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurypylus ("Broadgate") was the son of Telephus, king of Mysia. He was a great warrior, who led a Mysian contingent that fought alongside the Trojans against the Greeks in the Trojan War.

Q122248.label: Heracles
Q122248.description: divine hero in Greek mythology, son of Zeus and Alcmene
Q122248.lead: Heracles, born Alcaeus (Ἀλκαῖος) or Alcides (Ἀλκείδης), was the greatest of the Greek heroes. He was considered the son of Zeus and Alcmene, and the foster son of Amphitryon.

Q128176.label: Agamemnon
Q128176.description: son of Atreus in Greek mythology
Q128176.lead: In Greek mythology, Agamemnon was a king of Mycenae who commanded the Achaeans during the Trojan War. He was the son (or grandson) of King Atreus and Queen Aerope, the brother of Menelaus, the husband of Clytemnestra, and the father of Iphigenia, Iphianassa, Electra, Laodike, Orestes and Chrysothemis.

Q130818.label: Atlas
Q130818.lead: In Greek mythology, Atlas is a Titan condemned to hold up the heavens or sky for eternity after the Titanomachy. Atlas also plays a role in the myths of two of the greatest Greek heroes: Heracles (Hercules in Roman mythology) and Perseus.

Q131090.label: Chaos
Q131090.lead: In the context of religious cosmogony, Chaos refers to the division of reality outside or in contrast to the ordered cosmos. As such it refers to a state, place, or time beyond the known, familiar, and reliable world, often said to be inhabited by strange, ominous, or demonic beings.

Q131585.label: Selene
Q131585.description: ancient Greek goddess and personification of the Moon, daughter of Hyperion and Theia
Q131585.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Selene is the goddess and personification of the Moon. Also known as Mene (Ancient Greek: μήνη pronounced [mɛ̌ː.nɛː] MEH-neh), she is traditionally the daughter of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, and sister of the sun god Helios and the dawn goddess Eos.

Q131588.label: Ganymede
Q131588.description: son of Tros in Greek mythology
Q131588.lead: In Greek mythology, Ganymede ( GAN-im-eed) or Ganymedes is a divine hero whose homeland was Troy. Homer describes Ganymede as the most handsome of mortals and tells the story of how he was abducted by the gods to serve as Zeus's cup-bearer in Olympus.

Q1320718.label: Theseus
Q1320718.description: legendary king of Athens, son of Aegeus and Aethra; famous for slaying the Minotaur
Q1320718.lead: Theseus was a divine hero in Greek mythology, famous for slaying the Minotaur. The myths surrounding Theseus, his journeys, exploits, and friends, have provided material for storytelling throughout the ages.

Q1330532.label: Lycomedes
Q1330532.description: king of Scyros in Greek mythology
Q1330532.lead: In Greek mythology, Lycomedes, also known as Lycurgus, was the most prominent king of the Dolopians in the island of Scyros near Euboea during the Trojan War.

Q1378566.label: Eurysaces
Q1378566.description: son of Ajax the Great in Greek mythology
Q1378566.lead: Eurysaces in Greek mythology was the son of the Ajax and the enslaved former Teuthranian princess Tecmessa. He was venerated in Athens.

Q140001.label: Eris
Q140001.lead: In Greek mythology, Eris is the goddess and personification of strife and discord, particularly in war, and in the Iliad (where she is the "sister" of Ares the god of war). According to Hesiod she was the daughter of primordial Nyx (Night), and the mother of a long list of undesirable personified abstractions, such as Ponos (Toil), Limos (Famine), Algea (Pains) and Ate (Delusion).

Q15711586.label: Cymothoe
Q15711586.lead: In Greek mythology, Cymothoë was the "cerulean" Nereid of gentle and quiet waves. She was a marine-nymph daughter of the "Old Man of the Sea" Nereus and the Oceanid Doris.

Q159168.label: Themis
Q159168.description: in ancient Greek mythology, a titaness, the personification of divine order, fairness, law, natural law, and custom, whose symbols are the scales of justice
Q159168.lead: In Greek mythology and religion, Themis is the goddess and personification of justice, divine order, law, and custom. She is one of the twelve Titan children of Gaia and Uranus, and the second wife of Zeus.

Q159666.label: Hector
Q159666.description: prince of Troy in Greek mythology
Q159666.lead: In Greek mythology, Hector was a Trojan prince, a hero, and the greatest warrior for Troy during the Trojan War. He is a major character in Homer's Iliad, where he leads the Trojans and their allies in the defense of Troy, killing countless Greek warriors.

Q161419.label: Oceanus
Q161419.description: ancient Greek god of the earth-encircling river, Oceanos
Q161419.lead: In Greek mythology, Oceanus or Okeanos was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth), and the god of the great river which encircled the entire world. He was the brother and husband of the Titaness Tethys, and by her was the father of the river gods and the Oceanids.

Q164061.label: Helen of Troy
Q164061.description: daughter of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q164061.lead: Helen, commonly known as Helen of Troy and sometimes as Helen of Sparta, is a figure in Greek mythology said to have been the most beautiful woman in the world. She was believed to have been the daughter of Zeus by Leda or Nemesis, and the sister of Clytemnestra, Castor, Pollux, Philonoe, Phoebe and Timandra.

Q167646.label: Paris
Q167646.description: mythological son of Priam, king of Troy
Q167646.lead: Paris, also known as Alexander (Ancient Greek: Ἀλέξανδρος, romanized: Aléxandros), is a figure from Greek mythology who appears in the numerous stories about the Trojan War, including the Iliad. He was prince of Troy, son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba, and younger brother of Prince Hector.

Q1686620.label: Eumelus
Q1686620.description: mythical king of Pherae, son of Admetus

Q170473.label: Priam
Q170473.description: the legendary and last king of Troy during the Trojan war; son of Laomedon
Q170473.lead: In Greek mythology, Priam was the legendary and last king of Troy during the Trojan War. He was the son of Laomedon.

Q170779.label: Cassandra
Q170779.description: mythological prophetess and princess of Troy
Q170779.lead: In Greek mythology, Cassandra, also spelled Kassandra or Casandra, was a Trojan priestess dedicated to the god Apollo and fated by him to utter true prophecies, but never to be believed. Cassandra lived through the Trojan War and survived the sack of the city, but was murdered by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus when Agamemnon brought her to Mycenae as a pallake.

Q171839.label: Menelaus
Q171839.description: mythical king of Sparta, husband of Helen of Troy
Q171839.lead: In Greek mythology, Menelaus was a king of Sparta. According to the Iliad, the Trojan War began as a result of Menelaus' wife, Helen, fleeing to Troy with the Trojan prince Paris.

Q172549.label: Aeolus
Q172549.description: god of winds, son of Hippotes in Greek mythology
Q172549.lead: In Greek mythology, Aeolus, the son of Hippotes, was the ruler of the winds encountered by Odysseus in Homer's Odyssey. Aeolus was the king of the island of Aeolia, where he lived with his wife and six sons and six daughters.

Q172725.label: Ajax the Great
Q172725.description: son of Telamon in Greek mythology
Q172725.lead: Ajax or Aias is a Greek mythological hero, the son of King Telamon and Periboea, and the half-brother of Teucer.

Q174353.label: Orpheus
Q174353.description: legendary musician, poet, and prophet in ancient Greek religion and myth
Q174353.lead: In Greek mythology, Orpheus was a Thracian bard, legendary musician and prophet. He was also a renowned poet and, according to legend, travelled with Jason and the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece, and descended into the underworld to recover his lost wife, Eurydice.

Q178417.label: Eos
Q178417.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Eos is the goddess and personification of the dawn, who rose each morning from her home at the edge of the river Oceanus to deliver light and disperse the night. She opened the gates of heaven for her brother Helios (the Sun), to pass through, and was imagined in poetry and art as a radiant, often winged goddess driving her horse-drawn chariot across the sky, bringing with her the colours and dew of morning.

Q1784620.label: Coroebus
Q1784620.lead: In Greek mythology, Coroebus may refer to three distinct characters: Coroebus, son of King Mygdon of Phrygia and Axanimene, is a character of Greek legend. He came to the aid of Troy during the Trojan War out of love for Princess Cassandra.

Q178641.label: Peleus
Q178641.description: son of Aeacus in Greek mythology
Q178641.lead: In Greek mythology, Peleus was a hero, king of Phthia, husband of Thetis and the father of their son Achilles.

Q179209.label: Hyperion
Q179209.lead: In Greek mythology, Hyperion was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). With his sister, the Titaness Theia, Hyperion fathered Helios (Sun), Selene (Moon) and Eos (Dawn).

Q179543.label: Iapetos
Q179543.lead: In Greek mythology, Iapetus or Iapetos, also Japetus or Japetos, was one of the Titans, the son of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth) and father of Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus, and Menoetius. He was also called the father of Buphagus and Anchiale in other sources.

Q182019.label: Leda
Q182019.description: daughter of Thestius in Greek mythology
Q182019.lead: In Greek mythology, Leda, also rendered as Lede, was an Aetolian princess who became queen consort of Sparta through her marriage to King Tyndareus. Zeus fell in love with Leda, and to avoid his wife Hera's jealousy, assaulted her while disguised as a swan.

Q182837.label: Coeus
Q182837.description: Titan in Greek mythology, one of the twelve titans
Q182837.lead: In Greek mythology, Coeus, also called Koios or Polus, was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth).

Q183281.label: Phoebe
Q183281.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Phoebe was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She is a goddess of intellect and prophecy.

Q184216.label: Tethys
Q184216.description: ancient Greek mythological figure; mother of the river gods and the Oceanids
Q184216.lead: In Greek mythology, Tethys was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth), the sister and wife of the Titan Oceanus, and the mother of the river gods and the Oceanids. Although Tethys had no active role in Greek mythology and no established cults, she was depicted in mosaics decorating baths, pools, and triclinia in the Greek East, particularly in Antioch and its suburbs, either alone or with Oceanus.

Q184232.label: Theia
Q184232.description: female Titan in Greek mythology; mother of Helios, Selene and Eos
Q184232.lead: In Greek mythology, Theia also called Thea, Thia, Euryphaessa, Aethra or Basileia, was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). Her brother-husband is Hyperion, a god of the light, and together they are the parents of Helios (the Sun), Selene (the Moon), and Eos (the Dawn).

Q184437.label: Thetis
Q184437.lead: Thetis is a figure from Greek mythology with varying mythological roles. She mainly appears as a sea nymph, a goddess of water, and one of the 50 Nereids, daughters of the ancient sea god Nereus.

Q184570.label: Iris
Q184570.description: the personification of the rainbow in ancient Greek religion and mythology
Q184570.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Iris is a daughter of the gods Thaumas and Electra, and the personification of the rainbow. She functions as a messenger and servant to the Olympians, particularly Hera.

Q189527.label: Nereus
Q189527.lead: In Greek mythology, Nereus was the eldest son of Pontus (the Sea) and Gaia (the Earth). Nereus and Doris became the parents of 50 daughters (the Nereids) and a son (Nerites), with whom Nereus lived in the Aegean Sea.

Q190563.label: Pontus
Q190563.lead: In Greek mythology, Pontus is the personification of the sea. In Hesiod's Theogony (8th or 7th century BC), he is the offspring of Gaia (the Earth), who produces him alone.

Q190565.label: Metis
Q190565.description: Oceanid of Greek mythology, goddess of wisdom, daughter of Oceanid and Tethys
Q190565.lead: Metis, in ancient Greek religion and mythology, was the pre-Olympian goddess of wisdom, counsel and deep thought, and a member of the Oceanids. She is notable for being the advisor and first wife of Zeus, the king of the gods.

Q191725.label: Aegeus
Q191725.lead: Aegeus was one of the kings of Athens in Greek mythology, who gave his name to the Aegean Sea, was the father of Theseus, and founded Athenian institutions.

Q192469.label: Atreus
Q192469.description: king of Mycenae, father of Agamemnon
Q192469.lead: In Greek mythology, Atreus was a king of Mycenae in the Peloponnese, the son of Pelops and Hippodamia, and the father of Agamemnon and Menelaus. His descendants became known collectively as the Atreidae (Ancient Greek: Ἀτρείδαι Atreidai).

Q193267.label: Nestor
Q193267.description: wise ruler of Pylos in Greek mythology, son of Neleus
Q193267.lead: In Greek mythology, Nestor of Gerenia was a legendary king of Pylos. He is a prominent secondary character in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, where he appears as an elderly warrior who frequently offers advice to the other characters.

Q193433.label: Hecuba
Q193433.lead: In Greek mythology, Hecuba was the wife of King Priam and queen of Troy during the Trojan War. With Priam, she was the mother of the warriors Hector and Troilus; Helen's suitor Paris; and the prophetess Cassandra.

Q19376.label: Andromache
Q19376.description: wife of Hector in Greek mythology
Q19376.lead: In Greek mythology, Andromache was the wife of Hector, daughter of Eetion, and sister to Podes. She was born and raised in the city of Cilician Thebe, over which her father ruled.

Q19946249.label: Eurymachus
Q19946249.description: son of Antenor in Greek mythology

Q199923.label: Dione
Q199923.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Dione is an oracular goddess and Titaness. She is primarily known from Book V of Homer's Iliad, where she tends to the wounds suffered by her daughter Aphrodite.

Q20113799.label: Antibrote
Q20113799.lead: In Greek mythology, Antibrote was one of the Amazons, a race of warrior-women. She was one of Penthesilea's twelve companions at Troy.

Q208256.label: Diomedes
Q208256.description: hero son of Tydeus in Greek mythology, king of Argos
Q208256.lead: Diomedes or Diomede is a hero in Greek mythology, known for his participation in the Trojan War. He was born to Tydeus and Deipyle and later became King of Argos, succeeding his maternal grandfather, Adrastus.

Q211953.label: Anchises
Q211953.description: father of Aeneas in Greek mythology, lover of Aphrodite
Q211953.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Anchises was a member of the royal family of Troy. He was said to have been the son of King Capys of Dardania and Themiste, daughter of Ilus, who was son of Tros.

Q212827.label: Philoctetes
Q212827.lead: Philoctetes or Philocthetes, according to Greek mythology, was the son of Poeas, king of Meliboea in Thessaly, and Demonassa or Methone. He was a Greek hero, famed as an archer, and a participant in the Trojan War.

Q2276869.label: Pallas
Q2276869.description: mythical Greek deity, daughter of Triton
Q2276869.lead: In Greek mythology, Pallas was a warrior and childhood friend of the goddess Athena.

Q2300199.label: Meges
Q2300199.lead: In Greek mythology, Mégês Phyleïdês was the commander of Epeans and/or Dulichians during the Trojan War.

Q2436714.label: Tisiphone
Q2436714.description: daughter of Alcmaeon in Greek mythology
Q2436714.lead: In Greek mythology, Tisiphone is the daughter of Alcmaeon, Argive hero and one of the Epigoni, and Manto, the daughter of Tiresias. As an infant Tisiphone was given to the care of the royal couple of Corinth, but as she grew up the queen sold her as slave, envious of her great beauty.

Q244318.label: Briseis
Q244318.description: daughter of Briseus in Greek mythology
Q244318.lead: Briseis, also known as Hippodameia (Ἱπποδάμεια, [hippodámeːa]), is a significant character in the Iliad. Her role as a status symbol is at the heart of the dispute between Achilles and Agamemnon that initiates the plot of Homer's epic.

Q2479077.label: Simoeis
Q2479077.description: god of the Simoeis river, Troad
Q2479077.lead: Simoeis or Simois was a river of the Trojan plain, now called the Dümruk Su (Dümrek Çayı), and the name of its god in Greek mythology.

Q250506.label: Tydeus
Q250506.description: son of Oeneus in Greek mythology
Q250506.lead: Tydeus was an Aetolian hero in Greek mythology, belonging to the generation before the Trojan War. He was one of the Seven against Thebes, and the father of Diomedes, who is frequently known by the patronymic Tydides.

Q254381.label: Peneleus
Q254381.description: son of Hippalcimus in Greek mythology
Q254381.lead: In Greek mythology, Peneleos or, less commonly, Peneleus (Πηνέλεος Pēnéleos), son of Hippalcimus (Hippalmus) and Asterope, was an Achaean soldier in the Trojan War.

Q2547185.label: Agenor
Q2547185.lead: In Greek mythology, Agenor was a Trojan hero.

Q272047.label: Endymion
Q272047.description: son of Aethlius in Greek mythology
Q272047.lead: In Greek mythology, Endymion was variously a handsome Aeolian shepherd, hunter, or king who was said to rule and live at Olympia in Elis. He was also venerated and said to reside on Mount Latmus in Caria, on the west coast of Asia Minor.

Q2723576.label: Podarge
Q2723576.description: one of the Harpies in Greek mythology
Q2723576.lead: In Greek mythology, Podarge is a harpy, a personification of a swift wind and mate of Zephyrus, the West Wind. She is the mother of Balius and Xanthus — two divine horses renowned for their swiftness and who were gifted to Achilles, running as fast as the wind.

Q278930.label: Epeius
Q278930.description: mythical character, Achean soldier who built the Trojan Horse
Q278930.lead: Epeius or Epeus was a mythological Greek soldier during the Trojan War or, in some accounts, one of the Achaean Leaders, at the head of a contingent of 30 ships from the islands of the Cyclades. He was also the architect of the Wooden Horse, by means of which the Achaeans took Troy; he was himself among those warriors who hid inside it.

Q322639.label: Neoptolemus
Q322639.lead: In Greek mythology, Neoptolemus, originally called Pyrrhus at birth (Πύρρος, Pýrrhos, 'red'), was the son of the mythical warrior Achilles and the princess Deidamia, and the brother of Oneiros. He became the progenitor of the ruling dynasty of the Molossians of ancient Epirus.

Q331327.label: Telamon
Q331327.description: one of the Argonauts of Jason, in Greek mythology
Q331327.lead: Telamon in Greek mythology was the son of King Aeacus of Aegina, and Endeïs, a mountain nymph. The elder brother of Peleus, Telamon sailed alongside Jason as one of his Argonauts, and was present at the hunt for the Calydonian Boar.

Q332324.label: Laomedon
Q332324.lead: In Greek mythology, Laomedon was a Trojan king, son of Ilus and thus nephew of Ganymede and Assaracus. Laomedon was variously identified with different parents and siblings, as well as numerous children, including Priam and Tithonus.

Q3342132.label: Nireus
Q3342132.description: mythological Greek character, son of Poseidon

Q334787.label: Astyanax
Q334787.lead: In Greek mythology, Astyanax was the son of Hector, the crown prince of Troy, and of his wife, Princess Andromache of Cilician Thebe. His birth name was Scamandrius (in Greek: Σκαμάνδριος Skamandrios, after the river Scamander), but the people of Troy nicknamed him Astyanax (i.e.

Q34201.label: Zeus
Q34201.description: Greek god of the sky and king of the gods
Q34201.lead: Zeus is the supreme deity of the Greek pantheon. He is a sky and thunder god in ancient Greek religion and mythology, who rules as king of the gods on Mount Olympus.

Q348668.label: Acamas
Q348668.lead: In Greek mythology, Acamas or Akamas was a hero in the Trojan War.

Q35500.label: Aphrodite
Q35500.description: Greek goddess of love, beauty, pleasure, and procreation
Q35500.lead: Aphrodite is an ancient Greek goddess associated with love and beauty. Aphrodite's main cult centers were Cythera, Cyprus, Corinth, and Athens.

Q3564532.label: Alcibie
Q3564532.lead: In Greek Mythology Alcibie was one of the Amazons, a race of warrior-women. She fought with their queen, Penthesilea to the Trojan War.

Q3644221.label: Bremusa
Q3644221.lead: In Greek Mythology, Bremusa was one of a group of 12 Amazonian warriors. She was born in Themiskyra in 1204 BC and fought with Penthesilea.

Q367819.label: Meriones
Q367819.description: mythical son of Molus of Crete
Q367819.lead: Meriones was the Cretan son of Molus and Melphis or Euippe in Greek mythology. Molus was a half-brother of Idomeneus.

Q3680504.label: Cleodorus
Q3680504.lead: In Greek mythology, Cleodorus was a Rhodian soldier during the Trojan War who was shot to death by Paris, son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba of Troy. Cleodorus himself was the son of Lernus and Amphiale.

Q3705857.label: Derinoe
Q3705857.description: one of the Amazons, a race of warrior-women
Q3705857.lead: In Greek mythology, Derinoe was one of the Amazons, a race of warrior-women. She came with their queen, Penthesilia to the Trojan War.

Q37122.label: Athena
Q37122.description: goddess of wisdom and war in ancient Greek religion and mythology
Q37122.lead: Athena or Athene, often given the epithet Pallas, is an ancient Greek goddess associated with wisdom, warfare, and handicraft who was later syncretised with the Roman goddess Minerva and Etruscan Menrva. Athena was regarded as the patron and protectress of various cities across Greece, particularly the city of Athens, from which she most likely received her name.

Q37340.label: Apollo
Q37340.description: god in Greek and later Roman mythology
Q37340.lead: Apollo is one of the Olympian deities in ancient Greek religion and mythology. His numerous functions include light, healing, prophecy, music, poetry, and archery.

Q38012.label: Hera
Q38012.description: Greek goddess, wife and sister of Zeus
Q38012.lead: In ancient Greek religion, Hera is the goddess of marriage, women, and family, and the protector of women during childbirth. In Greek mythology, she is queen among the twelve Olympians on Mount Olympus, sister and wife of Zeus, and daughter of the Titans Cronus and Rhea.

Q3892897.label: Pammon
Q3892897.description: son of Priam in Greek mythology
Q3892897.lead: In Greek mythology, Pammon was a Trojan prince and one of the sons of King Priam of Troy and Hecuba. He was killed by Achilles' son Neoptolemus during the Trojan War.

Q390492.label: Agapenor
Q390492.description: son of Ancaeus in Greek mythology
Q390492.lead: In Greek mythology, Agapenor was a leader of the Arcadians in the Trojan War.

Q3995914.label: Toxaechmes
Q3995914.lead: In Greek mythology, Toxaechmes was the "stalwart" Achaean warrior who participated in the Trojan War.

Q40901.label: Ares
Q40901.description: Greek god of war and combat
Q40901.lead: Ares is the Greek god of war and courage. He is one of the Twelve Olympians, and the son of Zeus and Hera.

Q41127.label: Poseidon
Q41127.description: one of the twelve Olympians presiding over the sea, storms, earthquakes and horses
Q41127.lead: Poseidon is one of the twelve Olympians in ancient Greek religion and mythology, presiding over the sea, storms, earthquakes and horses. He was the protector of seafarers and the guardian of many Hellenic cities and colonies.

Q41484.label: Hermes
Q41484.description: Olympian god in Greek religion and mythology; the emissary and messenger of the gods; the god of trade, heraldry, merchants, commerce, roads, thieves, trickery, sports, travelers, and athletes; the son of Zeus and the Pleiad Maia
Q41484.lead: Hermes is an Olympian deity in ancient Greek religion and mythology considered the herald of the gods. He is also widely considered the protector of human heralds, travelers, thieves, merchants, and orators.

Q41746.label: Achilles
Q41746.description: Greek mythological hero of the Trojan War
Q41746.lead: In Greek mythology, Achilles or Achilleus (Ancient Greek: Ἀχιλλεύς, romanized: Achilleús) was a hero of the Trojan War who was known as being the greatest of all the Greek warriors. The central character in Homer's Iliad, he was the son of the Nereid Thetis and Peleus, king of Phthia and famous Argonaut.

Q431387.label: Deidamia
Q431387.description: Greek mythological figure, daughter of Lycomedes
Q431387.lead: In Greek mythology, Deidamia is a daughter of King Lycomedes, who lives on the island of Scyros. She marries Achilles, by whom she becomes the mother of Neoptolemus.

Q44204.label: Cronus
Q44204.description: ruler of the Titans in Greek mythology
Q44204.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Cronus, Cronos, or Kronos was the leader and youngest of the Titans, the children of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky). Cronus castrated and overthrew his father and then ruled during the mythological Golden Age until he himself was overthrown by his son, Zeus, and imprisoned in Tartarus.

Q44384.label: Hephaestus
Q44384.lead: Hephaestus is the Greek god of artisans, blacksmiths, carpenters, craftsmen, fire, metallurgy, metalworking, sculpture, and volcanoes. In Greek mythology, Hephaestus was the son of Hera, either on her own or by her husband Zeus.

Q461212.label: Dardanus
Q461212.description: mythological Greek character, son of Zeus
Q461212.lead: In Greek mythology, Dardanus was the founder of the city of Dardanus at the foot of Mount Ida in the Troad. Dardanus, a son of Zeus and the Pleiad Electra, was a significant figure in Greek mythology.

Q463865.label: Pleione
Q463865.lead: Pleione was an Oceanid nymph in Greek mythology and mother of the Pleiades. Pleione presided over the multiplication of the flocks, fitting, since the meaning of her name is: "to increase in number" (from the Greek word pleiôn πλεῖων "more").

Q47231.label: Odysseus
Q47231.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Odysseus, also known by the Latin variant Ulysses (UK also ; Latin: Ulysses, Ulixes), is a legendary Greek king of Ithaca and the hero of Homer's epic poem, the Odyssey. Odysseus also plays a key role in Homer's Iliad and other works in that same epic cycle.

Q474888.label: Amphilochus
Q474888.lead: In Greek mythology, Amphilochus was an Argive hero and one of the Epigoni.

Q4770957.label: Antandre
Q4770957.lead: In Greek mythology, Antandre was an Amazonian warrior. She was one of the Penthesilea's twelve companions at Troy.

Q506781.label: Memnon
Q506781.description: mythical Ethiopian king, son of Tithonus and Eos
Q506781.lead: In Greek mythology, Memnon was a king of Aethiopia and son of Tithonus and Eos. During the Trojan War, he brought an army to Troy's defense and killed Antilochus, Nestor's son, during a fierce battle.

Q508543.label: Aerope
Q508543.description: daughter of Catreus, the king of Crete
Q508543.lead: In Greek mythology, Aerope was a Cretan princess as the daughter of Catreus, king of Crete. She was the sister of Clymene, Apemosyne and Althaemenes.

Q570434.label: Idomeneus
Q570434.description: Greek mythical character, King of Crete
Q570434.lead: In Greek mythology, Idomeneus was a Cretan king and commander who led the Cretan armies to the Trojan War, in eighty black ships. He was also one of the suitors of Helen, as well as a comrade of the Telamonian Ajax.

Q571969.label: Antenor
Q571969.lead: In Greek mythology, Antenor was a counselor to King Priam of Troy during the events of the Trojan War.

Q577552.label: Antilochus
Q577552.lead: In Greek mythology, Antilochus was a prince of Pylos and one of the Achaeans in the Trojan War. He was the youngest prince to command troops.

Q6081853.label: Polites
Q6081853.description: mythological Greek character, Trojan prince, son of Priam
Q6081853.lead: In Greek mythology, Polites was the legitimate son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba, known for his swiftness. He was a brother of 49 other children.

Q652220.label: Alcathous
Q652220.description: Greek mythical character, son of Aesyetes

Q658523.label: Hermione
Q658523.description: daughter of Menelaus and Helen of Troy
Q658523.lead: In Greek mythology, Hermione was the daughter of Menelaus, king of Sparta, and his wife, Helen of Troy. Prior to the Trojan War, Hermione had been betrothed by Tyndareus, her grandfather, to her cousin Orestes, son of her uncle, Agamemnon.

Q66016.label: Muse
Q66016.description: goddess of the inspiration of literature, science and the arts
Q66016.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, the Muses were the inspirational goddesses of literature, science, and the arts. They were considered the source of the knowledge embodied in the poetry, lyric songs, and myths that were related orally for centuries in ancient Greek culture.

Q663792.label: Sinon
Q663792.description: son of Aesimus in Greek mythology
Q663792.lead: In Greek mythology, Sinon or Sinopos was a Greek warrior during the Trojan War. He is not mentioned by Homer, but his story as given in Virgil's Aeneid and other accounts presents him as a treacherous agent of the Greeks who misleads the Trojans and encourages them to bring the Trojan Horse inside the city.

Q674319.label: Machaon
Q674319.description: character of Greek mythology: son of Asclepius and Coronis, lover of Anticlea; healing hero of the Trojan War; killed by Eurypylus
Q674319.lead: In Greek mythology, Machaon was a son of Asclepius; and the older brother of Podalirius. He and his brother led an army from Tricca in the Trojan War on the side of the Greeks.

Q725286.label: Coronis
Q725286.description: goddess from Greek mythology: princess, daughter of Phlegyas, lover of Ischys and Apollo, mother of Asclepius; killed by Apollon and Artemis
Q725286.lead: In Greek mythology, Coronis is a Thessalian princess and a lover of the god Apollo. She was the daughter of Cleophema and Phlegyas, king of the Lapiths.

Q725527.label: Calchas
Q725527.lead: Calchas is an Argive mantis, or seer, in Greek mythology. Calchas appears in the opening scenes of the Iliad and also has a long literary history after Homer.

Q726279.label: Doris
Q726279.lead: Doris, in Greek mythology, was a sea goddess. She was one of the 3,000 Oceanids, daughters of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys.

Q729332.label: Helenus
Q729332.lead: In Greek mythology, Helenus was a gentle and clever seer. He was also a Trojan prince as the son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba of Troy, and the twin brother of the prophetess Cassandra.

Q736813.label: Deiphobus
Q736813.description: mythical character, son of Priam of Troy
Q736813.lead: In Greek mythology, Deiphobus was a son of Priam and Hecuba. He was a prince of Troy, and the greatest of Priam's sons after Hector.

Q737306.label: Tithonus
Q737306.description: prince of Troy loved by Eos in Greek mythology
Q737306.lead: In Greek mythology, Tithonus was the lover of Eos, Goddess of the Dawn. He was a prince of Troy, the son of King Laomedon by the Naiad Strymo (Στρυμώ).

Q747657.label: Enyo
Q747657.description: Greek goddess of war and destruction
Q747657.lead: In Greek mythology, Enyo is a war-goddess, frequently associated with the war-god Ares. The Romans identified her with Bellona.

Q750580.label: Pittheus
Q750580.description: son of Pelops in Greek mythology
Q750580.lead: In Greek mythology, Pittheus was the king of Troezen, city in Argolis, which he had named after his brother Troezen.

Q760213.label: Auge
Q760213.description: daughter of Aleus in Greek mythology
Q760213.lead: In Greek mythology, Auge, was the daughter of Aleus the king of Tegea in Arcadia, and the virgin priestess of Athena Alea. She was also the mother of the hero Telephus by Heracles.

Q772808.label: Automedon
Q772808.description: son of Diores and charioteer of Achilles
Q772808.lead: In Greek mythology, Automedon, son of Diores, was Achilles' charioteer, who drove the immortal horses Balius and Xanthos. He was from the island of Skyros.

Q79999.label: Uranus
Q79999.description: primordial Greek deity, god of the Sky; one of the Greek primordial deities
Q79999.lead: In Greek mythology, Uranus, sometimes written Ouranos (Ancient Greek: Οὐρανός, lit. 'sky', [uːranós]), is the personification of the sky and one of the Greek primordial deities. According to Hesiod, Uranus was the son and husband of Gaia (Earth), with whom he fathered the first generation of Titans.

Q82732.label: Aeneas
Q82732.description: Trojan hero, son of Anchises and Aphrodite
Q82732.lead: Aeneas was a Trojan hero in Greco-Roman mythology, the son of the Trojan prince Anchises and the Greek goddess Aphrodite (equivalent to the Roman Venus). His father was a first cousin of King Priam of Troy (both being great-grandsons of Tros, founder of Troy), making Aeneas a second cousin to Priam's children (such as Hector and Paris).

Q83160.label: Prometheus
Q83160.description: Titan, culture hero, and trickster figure in Greek mythology who defied the gods; son of Iapetus
Q83160.lead: In Greek mythology, Prometheus is a Titan who is responsible for creating and aiding humanity in its earliest days. He defied the Olympian gods by stealing fire from them and giving it to humanity.

Q83223.label: Asclepius
Q83223.lead: Asclepius is a hero and god of medicine in ancient Greek religion and mythology. He is the son of Apollo and Coronis, or Arsinoe, or of Apollo alone.

Q833826.label: Nauplius
Q833826.description: king of Nauplia, son of Poseidon in Greek mythology

Q836792.label: Klymene
Q836792.lead: In Greek mythology, Clymene or Klymene is the name of one of the three thousand Oceanid nymphs, usually the wife of Iapetus and mother by him of Prometheus, Epimetheus, Atlas and Menoetius.

Q858663.label: Electra
Q858663.description: one of the Pleiades in Greek mythology
Q858663.lead: In Greek mythology, Electra was one of the Pleiades, the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione. She lived on the island of Samothrace.

Q858671.label: Oenone
Q858671.description: nymph of Greek mythology, wife of Paris
Q858671.lead: In Greek mythology, Oenone was the first wife of Paris of Troy, whom he abandoned for Helen. Oenone was also the ancient name of an island, which was later named after Aegina, daughter of the river god Asopus.

Q878184.label: Teucer
Q878184.lead: In Greek mythology, Teucer, was the son of King Telamon of Salamis Island and his second wife Hesione, daughter of King Laomedon of Troy. He fought alongside his half-brother, Ajax, in the Trojan War and is the legendary founder of the city of Salamis on Cyprus.

Q916442.label: Telephus
Q916442.lead: In Greek mythology, Telephus was the son of Heracles and Auge, who was the daughter of king Aleus of Tegea. He was adopted by Teuthras, the king of Mysia, in Asia Minor, whom he succeeded as king.

Q93172.label: Gaia
Q93172.description: Greek primordial deity, the personification of the Earth
Q93172.lead: In Greek mythology, Gaia, also spelled Gaea, is the personification of Earth. She is the mother of Uranus (Sky), with whom she conceived the Titans (themselves parents of many of the Olympian gods), the Cyclopes, and the Giants, as well as of Pontus (Sea), from whose union she bore the primordial sea gods.

Q956906.label: Thrasymedes
Q956906.lead: In Greek mythology, Thrasymedes was a prince of Pylos and a participant in the Trojan War.
